title: Session decay amortization and PPK reconciliation
summary: Working sheet to reconcile per‑token/per‑request economics by amortizing fixed costs across session decay profiles. Focus: how different session TTLs and request shapes move 'raw' PPK to a practical billable PPK after model load amortization, cache hits (prefix + KV), and microburst reserve carveouts.
purpose: Create a reusable amortization kernel that product and ops can use when proposing pricing SKU changes and when sizing reserve capacity for bursty customers.
assumptions: Model load (cold start) amortizable over N concurrent sessions within ttl window
Average model memory license and orchestration overhead mapped to $/GPU-hour; converted to $/token via throughput assumptions
Two cache layers: prefix cache (80% hit on identical prompts bucket) and KV cache for chat sessions (hit depends on session length and reuse)
Spot-available mix for hosted API remains 30% of capacity for the modeled region
Network and ingress costs excluded (handled in separate sheet)

calculation-notes: raw-ppk is calculated from amortized GPU time per token using throughput traces (tokens/sec) + per-hour infra amortization
$-per-session-load-amortized = model-load-cost-per-session / total_tokens_in_session ; model-load-cost-per-session = model-boot-cost * (1 - reuse_probability) / expected_concurrent_reuse
cache-savings-ppk = (prefix_hit_rate * prefix_saving_per_token + kv_hit_rate * kv_saving_per_token) averaged by request shape
We bucket sessions by observed TTL deciles from telemetry (Q3 2025). Use decile center values for sensitivity runs.
key_findings: Short chat sessions (TTL <=30min) can reduce effective PPK by ~25% vs raw-ppk due to KV cache reuse even though they have higher per-session load amortization compared to ultra-long sessions.
Single-shot calls (form submission / summarization) remain >2x more expensive after amortization — good candidates for pre-warming, batching, or routing to smaller quantized models.
Increasing prefix cache TTL from 5m to 20m shows non-linear returns: first 10m yields most hit-rate lift for templated prompts; beyond 20m marginal benefit drops sharply.

Microburst reserve carveouts (reserve capacity to handle 99th pct spikes) are a major driver of short-term PPK volatility; smoothing via small per-request surcharge or burst-buckets reduces margin erosion.
recommended_actions: Add a product SKU for 'session-optimized chat' that defaults to a 30m TTL and includes discounted PPK assumptions; test with 3 pilot customers for 8 weeks.
Implement a pre-warm API with optional session affinity (customer-configurable) for single-shot high-latency models; evidence shows 40%-60% per-request cost reduction for heavy single-shot workloads.
Adjust hosted API routing: route high single-shot percent traffic to compact variants (quantized/open-13b) when predicted token budget > X and latency SLO allows.
Work with SRE to instrument a 'session reuse' metric exposed in console and per-customer analytics pane to monitor realized amortization in production.
Run a Monte Carlo next: vary prefix hit-rate, kv hit-rate, and concurrent reuse between realistic bounds to produce 95% confidence PPK bands per bucket.
open_questions: What's the correct allocation for license amortization when customers pin specific model versions? (split evenly across pinned sessions or attribute to customer?)
Should we bill per-session flat fee for long-lived sessions instead of per-token to better align economics for streaming assistants?
How to incorporate multi-region routing penalties (cross-region cache misses) into the amortization kernel?
What guardrails for pre-warm abuse (clients open many ephemeral sessions to game amortization) should we enforce?
next_steps: Schedule 60min working session with SRE and Pricing on 2026-02-18 to align telemetry and expected reuse signals
Wire a small A/B test: 1% traffic apply pre-warm for single-shot heavy models and measure realized PPK over 2 weeks
Publish 'session reuse' metric in internal console and cut a short doc for Solutions Eng describing the new SKU assumptions
